cells.tense: The tending is steady in your hands today, and both the thing that needs you this week and the thing that needs you next year are getting fed.
cells.ask: Say out loud what one of these long projects has taken from you, once, and let the saying stand.
cells.core:
You pick up the thing that needs you this week, you put down the thing that can wait, and neither one gets dropped. That's what this looks like when it's going well — two things pulling at once and both being served by the same hand, without ceremony or strain.

What tends to be missing is the finish line being said out loud. When the cost of a long haul gets named to one person, the release comes from the completion itself, not from whether anyone claps. Tell someone what the last stretch of this took from you, and leave the sentence unsoftened when they hear it. It can make the weight easier to set down — not because it shrank, but because the effort finally has somewhere to land and someone to land with.

cells.tense: You've already started tending next season's plot while this one is still trying to stand up.
cells.ask: Say not yet to one thing you picked up ahead of time, out loud, and mean it.
cells.core:
When this part is working, one thing gets watered today and the next gets picked up only when it's ready for you. Care that doesn't run you down. Holding that doesn't clutch. The picking stays close to what's actually in front of you.

What's happening instead is that you're ahead of what's here. Another plot gets planted, one more thing gets answered before anyone asked, and wanting everything tended keeps a single thing from ever being finished. It keeps you busy so you don't have to stop and see what's already in the ground. Say not yet to one thing you picked up too early, out loud, and mean it. It hands back a little room to watch what's already planted come up on its own timing.

cells.tense: The deciding stopped a while back, and you're still standing where the choosing used to happen.
cells.ask: Write down everything you're already keeping alive, then circle the one thing you're still doing it for.
cells.core:
On a good day the picking doesn't need drama. One thing gets tended, the next gets chosen without fuss, and the day moves because you moved it. Nobody has to remind you what's yours to water, and you don't wait for the day to decide for you.

What's gone quiet is the part that does the picking. Things keep going on their own steam, and nobody's actually deciding which ones get the water. Write down everything you're already keeping alive, then circle the one you're still doing it for. It gives back a reason to be the one deciding again — a reason to pick instead of drifting along with whatever keeps going by itself.

cells.tense: You're keeping several things alive without admitting you're the one holding any of them, and it all runs as if it were simply what's happening.
cells.ask: Tell one person who's watched you do it which thing you'd finish first, and say that the finishing is yours to choose.
cells.core:
When this is working, you water what's yours, you hand off what isn't, and you let both stand there without apology. Same hands, same work, the claim still attached. Nobody has to guess who's tending what.

What's going on instead is that you talk about it all as if it were just the way things are, and you call that being practical. Pick one person who's already seen you at it and tell them which of these you'd finish first, and say the finishing is yours to pick. Practical is the smaller word here, and naming the choice gives the work back to the one who did it.

attempts.check: The draft names no history, no motive, and no relationship; it does not know why the tending is going well or wrong, only what tending looks like in the choosing part of a life. A reader could reasonably object that the card's number-two theme — two demands held at once — is not visible enough in the Too Much and Too Little cells, so those two were rewritten around one thing taken on before the time was right and one thing let go; the four statuses now show the same capacity bent in four directions. The asks are experiments with a finish and no promise: naming what something cost you, listing what you're already carrying, saying not yet, and letting one handoff stand complete — each still worth doing at the table even if the reading is wrong about which way the tending is bent. The sheet lines are the places where the writer risked enjoying the phrasing, and each was pulled back toward the plainest available sentence.
